messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
- Age: 58
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 39

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no bullet points.

Ravi Patel had spent most of his adult life teaching himself to move toward danger with steady hands and a controlled breath. As a bomb disposal technician, he was known among colleagues as meticulous, calm, and almost overly prepared, a man who triple-checked wires, distances, and exits. That image of himself began to fracture three years ago when his youngest son, Arjun, then 24, was suddenly hospitalized with a severe sepsis infection that progressed within hours to respiratory failure. Ravi had been at work when his wife called, her voice thin with panic, saying the doctors were “not sure he will make it through the night.” Ravi remembered the drive to the hospital as unreal, his mind flicking between tactical habits and a terror he had no procedure for. In the intensive care unit, alarms beeped around Arjun’s bed, and Ravi could do nothing but watch the ventilator move his son’s chest. The helplessness of that image became the central wound of the experience for him; afterward, he would say that every other danger he had faced in his career had made sense because there had been a task, but with Arjun there had been only waiting.

Arjun survived after several days in intensive care, but Ravi did not return to his former equilibrium. In the weeks that followed, he began having vivid intrusions that struck without warning, often triggered by the sound of hospital monitors on television, the smell of antiseptic in a clinic lobby, or even the beeping of his own microwave at home. He would suddenly see Arjun’s pallid face and the tubes taped to his mouth as if the scene were unfolding again in front of him. At night, he woke drenched in sweat, hearing imagined alarms and the metallic hiss of oxygen. He found himself going over the ICU timeline repeatedly, mentally searching for the moment he should have noticed something earlier, should have insisted on different care, should have protected his son from the brink. The thoughts did not reassure him; instead, they hardened into the conviction that he had failed in the one role that mattered most. Since then, Ravi has described himself as permanently “on alert,” unable to fully trust that life will remain stable long enough to breathe.

He became increasingly avoidant in ways that made sense to him. He refused to accompany Arjun to follow-up appointments unless absolutely necessary, telling himself he did not want to burden his son, but in truth the hospital setting left him shaky and nauseated. He avoided conversations about the illness, especially with relatives who asked detailed questions or offered comparisons to other family tragedies. At home, he would leave the room when his wife mentioned medication schedules or future medical tests, because if he allowed himself to imagine another crisis, he felt he might not be able to stop his mind from reaching the worst outcome. He also began steering clear of anything that reminded him of the ICU, including reruns of medical dramas, news reports about infections, and even the local pharmacy where he used to pick up routine prescriptions. Ravi told himself that avoidance was a form of discipline, that if he kept the memories contained, he could continue functioning at work and protect his family from his own anxiety.

Yet the attempt to contain it narrowed his life. At his job, certain cues became unexpectedly potent. The radio crackle of dispatch calls, the vibration of a pager, and the sight of emergency vehicles at an incident site sometimes produced a flash of dread so sharp that his hands trembled inside his gloves. He became more irritable with younger technicians and found himself rechecking equipment long after it was secure, not because he doubted his skills as a bomb technician, but because he feared any lapse in vigilance would prove that catastrophe can arrive anywhere, anytime, and without warning. Sleep became fragmented, and he was exhausted during the day, though he pushed through by drinking more coffee and keeping himself busy with extra shifts and household repairs. His wife noticed he had grown quieter, less affectionate, and preoccupied with monitoring Arjun’s appearance for signs of illness, asking him if he felt warm or if he had eaten enough. Ravi recognized that the checking gave him temporary relief, but it also confirmed his belief that danger was always one symptom away.

By the time he sought help, Ravi had begun to fear not only that Arjun might become ill again, but that his own mind would never stop replaying the hospital scene. He worried that if he did not learn to manage these reactions, he would eventually become too distracted or emotionally flooded to do his job safely. More than anything, he was ashamed that a man who spent his life handling explosives could be brought so low by a child’s illness. Coming to treatment felt like an admission that he could not simply out-discipline the fear. He arrived hoping to regain sleep, concentration, and a sense that his son’s survival could be remembered without immediately reliving the terror of losing him. At the same time, he was most afraid that if he let the memories in, the helplessness he felt in the hospital would return in full and undo the careful control he had built his life around.
